name: Bryn Celli Ddu
about: Late Neolithic passage tomb on Anglesey (Burrow's radiocarbon model: built 3074-2956 cal BC) with an east/north-east-facing stone-lined passage, roughly aligned on the midsummer sunrise, leading to a polygonal chamber of large slabs with a free-standing rounded blueschist pillar. It overlies, or is enlarged from, an earlier phase with an encircling ditch (c. 21 m across) and an inner ring of stones, usually read as a henge with a stone circle; whether there was a henge (outer bank) is debated. A ring of kerbstones c. 26 m across marks the edge of the final mound. Five Mesolithic postholes lie in front of the entrance. Excavated by W. J. Hemp in 1928-29 (Ministry of Works guardianship from 1923), after which the mound was rebuilt only around the passage and chamber: the modern mound is much smaller than the original, leaves the back of the chamber open to the air, and is held up in part by concrete roof supports. The carved Pattern Stone, found lying flat by the central pit behind the chamber, is in Amgueddfa Cymru (St Fagans); a cast stands upright behind the chamber near where it was found. Quotes are exact text of the cited pages (whitespace normalised); 'derived' marks values computed from quoted numbers or OSM geometry.

chamber_uprights.note: Six large uprights (Anwyl 1908, Pennant, Simple Wikipedia), drystone walling between and above them (Skinner, Grimes). Cadw's 'octagonal' suggests eight sides; the walling may make up the extra sides (not stated).

Pennant described one great roof stone near ten feet across; Anglesey History one large plus one smaller. Wikipedia: concrete roof supports were added at some point.

It was uprooted by the finder before 1802 and re-set upright after 1929.

modern_mound_extent.value: covers only the passage and chamber; back of chamber open
modern_mound_extent.note: The 1928-29 restoration rebuilt the mound only around the chamber and passage. Pegasus says it is about a quarter of the original size and stops about 15 m short of the kerb at the rear (enthusiast estimate; 15 m is more than the 13 m radius of the kerb, so at best rough). No measured diameter or height of the modern mound was found. The OSM outline of the site (way 919723575) is 28.7 m E-W by 26.7 m N-S, area 575 m², equal-area diameter 27.0 m (derived), so it traces the kerb ring, not the smaller modern mound.

cites.quote: was restored only around the chamber and passage

Three of the stones, visible within the cairn mound, are thought to be from the stone circle of that time.

central_pit_diameter_m.note: Pit at the centre of the earlier enclosure, behind the chamber; held a burnt human ear bone and was covered with a slab, the Pattern Stone lying beside it.

cites.quote: a pit, about 1m in diameter, was dug at the centre of the henge

phases.what: Row of five postholes in front of the later entrance, pine charcoal dated; sources disagree on the millennium.

cites.quote: Radiocarbon dating of pine charcoal from two of the pits, carried out in 2006, showed these to date from around 4000 BC
five sixth-millennium cal BC Mesolithic postholes (Burrow 2010)

phases.name: Enclosure / henge and stone circle
phases.date: c. 3000 BC (Wikipedia); 'later Neolithic around 5,000 years ago' (Cadw)
phases.what: Ditch c. 21 m across (bank disputed) round a ring of stones, central pit with an ear bone, Pattern Stone probably standing.

cites.quote: Around 3000 BC, a henge monument was constructed.
The monument seems to have begun in the later Neolithic around 5,000 years ago, as a ‘henge’ or a ritual enclosure.

phases.name: Passage tomb
phases.what: Passage and polygonal chamber; mound enlarged to the 26 m kerb (Burrow: two phases; Bradley: first a c. 15 m unrevetted mound, enlarged twice). Wikipedia's 'around 1,000 years after the henge' conflicts with Burrow's dates.

cites.quote: The result is a two phase model which shows the tomb to have been built between 3074 and 2956 cal bc
in its first phase it consisted of a circular unrevetted mound about 15m in diameter, containing a passage grave
Around 1,000 years after the henge was built, the site was radically altered.

phases.name: Bronze Age cairns nearby
phases.what: Cairn c. 50 m south, double kerb.

cites.quote: Radiocarbon dating has given a date of 1,900 BC

phases.name: Antiquarian damage
phases.what: Discovered by a farmer seeking stone a generation before 1802; the pillar uprooted; stones taken for walls.

cites.quote: he was told how the passage tomb had been discovered a generation before, by a farmer looking for useful stone

phases.name: Guardianship, excavation and restoration
phases.what: Hemp's excavation; pillar re-set; mound rebuilt over passage and chamber only; Pattern Stone to the museum and a cast set up.

cites.quote: First explored seriously 1865, the tomb was thoroughly excavated in 1928–29.
Baynes suggested that the landowner, Lord Anglesey, should turn the site over to the Commissioners for the Preservation of Ancient Monuments, which he did in 1923.
the earth and stone mound covering the passage and chamber was reinstated, but clearly there was much less material available than had been used originally
was first excavated in 1865 and then completely reconstructed in the 1920s

debate.claim: Henge first, then tomb (Hemp, O'Kelly 1969) or not a henge at all (Eogan 1983, Bradley 1998, Burrow 2010): the case rests on an outer bank, for which Burrow found no evidence; the 2015 ERT survey found a possible buried bank.

cites.quote: Hemps' original hypothesis, that the tomb was built within a ruined henge, is nowadays seen as problematic.

O’Kelly’s henge thesis rests on whether or not the ditch was accompanied by an external bank, for which there is no evidence, either as a positive feature, or from fill layers in the ditch (Burrow 2010).
Anomaly A, located in transects 1 and 2, represents a potential outer bank.

debate.claim: Number of stones in the inner circle: 17 (Wikipedia) vs 14 (Simple Wikipedia, pegasus); medievalheritage 'sixteen' damaged. Hemp's plan is needed to settle it.

cites.quote: A ring of 17 stones formed an oval
a circular array of 14 standing stones

debate.claim: Pillar height: 1.7 m (Coflein) vs some 2 m (Wikipedia). Pillar rock: blueschist (project) rather than petrified wood (Soskin and Bott).

cites.quote: a 1.7m high smoothed stone pillar
Two researchers, Rupert Soskin and Michael Bott recently suggested that the pillar standing within the chamber is in fact the petrified remains of a tree trunk.
This post argues that it is made from blueschist

debate.claim: Chamber width: 2.4 m (Cadw) vs 3 m at widest (Anglesey History) vs about 2 m (Simple Wikipedia); 'octagonal' (Cadw) vs six uprights (Anwyl, Pennant).

cites.quote: an octagonal chamber 8ft/2.4m across
3m across at its widest

debate.claim: Was the Pattern Stone part of the earlier phase (standing in the enclosure, buried by the tomb builders) or placed for the tomb? Wikipedia and Anglesey History: earlier, standing; HER: thought to belong to the later phase; Museum: deliberately hidden by the tomb's builders.

cites.quote: It is thought this would have stood upright within the henge, as the patterns cover both sides.
A pit and a decorated stone found beside it are also thought to belong to this later phase.
The builders of the tomb deliberately hid it from view.

plans.title: Hemp 1930, plan of the excavated monument (Archaeologia 80, 179-214; also Hemp 1931, Archaeologia Cambrensis 86, 216-58)
plans.licence: uncertain: published by the Society of Antiquaries of London; Hemp died 1962, so in copyright to 2032 unless it counts as Crown copyright (Hemp was Inspector of Ancient Monuments, Office of Works), which would have expired. Not to be traced until cleared. DOI not verified (Cambridge Core paywalled).
plans.what it shows: the definitive plan: passage and chamber stones, kerbs, ditch, inner stone circle positions, central pit, Pattern Stone, forecourt and postholes

plans.title: Lockyer 1909, Fig. 94 'Plan of Bryn Celli Ddu' (copied by Baynes from the Lukis plan in Archaeologia Cambrensis)
plans.licence: public domain (1909; the 1847/1860s source plan also public domain)
plans.what it shows: pre-excavation chamber and passage stones only; Lockyer notes the Arch. Camb. north arrow is 35° out, so orientation must not be taken from it

plans.title: Burrow 2010, phase plans and the longitudinal section at the solstice (redrawn from Hemp)
plans.licence: copyright (Prehistoric Society / CUP); paywalled; not traceable
plans.what it shows: two-phase construction, where the solstice light falls

plans.title: Griffiths et al. 2016, Figure 1 (phases redrawn from Burrow 2010) and Figure 2 (ERT transects)
plans.what it shows: the alternative first-phase layouts and the final phase

plans.title: OpenStreetMap ways 919723575 (site outline) and 1367245454 (passage footway)
plans.what it shows: kerb-ring outline (c. 27 m) and the passage line (53° outward); no stones

gaps: No modern measured passage azimuth, width or height, chamber height or modern-mound dimensions were found in an open source; Burrow 2010 (PPS 76, paywalled at Cambridge Core) and Hemp 1930 (Archaeologia 80, paywalled) hold them. Hemp's plan and sections would give every stone's position.

Welsh Journals Online (journals.library.wales) answers scripts with a Cloudflare challenge (HTTP 403), so Hemp 1931 (Archaeologia Cambrensis 86, 216-58), O'Kelly 1969 (Arch. Camb. 118, 17-48) and the 1847 description could not be quoted.
RCAHMW Anglesey Inventory (1937) is on the Internet Archive only as a restricted lending copy (inventoryofancie0000vari).
Positions and sizes of the individual inner-circle stones, kerbstones and passage/chamber uprights: not published in any reachable source; the number of circle stones is disputed (14 vs 17).
Coflein's page has no plan image licence statement reachable by script; its images (map.coflein.gov.uk plans mentioned by medievalheritage) are Crown copyright under RCAHMW's non-commercial licence.

The modern mound's diameter and height are not published; OSM maps only the kerb-ring outline. Its size would have to come from photos, the HeritageTogether/Stanford photogrammetry models or the 2015 laser scan (project blog), whose licences were not checked (a Sketchfab model of the replica Pattern Stone is on Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.10378632 under CC BY 4.0).
Which stone exactly the solstice light falls on: only 'a quartz-rich stone at the back of the tomb' (Burrow via British Archaeology 2006); which upright is not identified in open sources.
Cadw's guidebook text and the Cadw scheduled-monument full report (AN002) were not reachable by script; Cadw's /history subpage returned nothing.
Mesolithic posthole date conflict (c. 4000 BC per Wikipedia vs sixth millennium cal BC per Griffiths et al. citing Burrow 2010) could not be settled without Burrow 2010.
